content.summary_of_the_paper: The paper extends the work of Lie et al. (JMLR) 2022, which studied the approximation capabilities of a linear continuous-time RNN. Particularly, the submission examines the addition of a non-linear activation function and concludes that this does not improve not diminish the approximation abilities of the CT-RNN.
content.strength_and_weaknesses:
# Pros:
- The paper builds upon the established theoretical framework of Lie. et al. 2022 and adds novel results.
- The paper looks at non-linear components which are more practically relevant than the linear RNN considered in Lie et al. 2022, making the topic of the work, in principle, interesting for the ICLR audience.

# Cons:
My main issue with the work is the state dynamics of the CT-RNN considered in Eq (5), which is, in my opinion, less relevant than the linear RNN considered in Lie et al. 2022.
First, although it is non-linear due to the activation function, it is missing the additional linear mapping necessary for a universal approximation, according to Hornik et al. 1989. In practice, I believe one would either use a linear RNN to leverage its implicit regularization (i.e., that a linear system is learned) or rely on a "full" non-linear CT-RNN with at least the additional linear mapping of Hornik et al. 1989. Thus, the CT-RNN considered in Eq (5) falls in a niche.
Second, the activation function applied in Eq (5) restricts the value range of the derivative compared to linear RNN. Thus, I would find it not really surprising that this, at some point, limits the approximation capacity of the ODE.
content.clarity,_quality,_novelty_and_reproducib:
Overall, the paper is pretty clear, following the footsteps of Lie et al. 2022, and the results are novel.

**Question regarding Proposition 4.1:**
Given that a tanh is just a "rescale" sigmoid, I wonder how the sigmoid activation is affected by the Proposition. Especially in Figure 2, the hard_sigmoid seems to be working quite well.
content.summary_of_the_review: I think this work extends Lie et al. 2022 in a meaningful direction. The question for me is how significant this extension is, though. I am by no means an expert in this domain, however, from a practical perspective, I think the type of model considered is rather less relevant. From a theoretical contribution point of view and thus its impact on the field on approximation capabilities of neural networks, I cannot judge this submission due to being outside my core research area.

content.title: Reply to Reviewer nbcx
content.comment:
We thank the reviewers' nice comments. Since there is a problem with the proof (and the claim) in Section 4.2, although the main results in Sections 4.1 and 4.3 are still correct, this paper requires a major revision. We will withdraw this paper and further improve the result. 

> The state dynamics of the CT-RNN considered in Eq (5) are less relevant than the linear RNN considered in Li et al. 2022.

The RNN formulation considered in Eq (5) is the commonly used RNN structure - Elman RNN cell [](https://pytorch.org/docs/stable/generated/torch.nn.RNNCell.html)[](https://www.tensorflow.org/api_docs/python/tf/keras/layers/SimpleRNN). This is the standard implementation of almost all deep learning libraries such as PyTorch and TensorFlow. Previous work considers the linear activation case as a simplification, but Eq (5) is a general state dynamics. 

> First, although it is non-linear due to the activation function, it is missing the additional linear mapping necessary for a universal approximation, according to Hornik et al. 1989. In practice, I believe one would either use a linear RNN to leverage its implicit regularization (i.e., that a linear system is learned) or rely on a "full" non-linear CT-RNN with at least the additional linear mapping of Hornik et al. 1989.

The Hornik 1989 paper is not considering the universal approximation of RNN. The main results in Hornik 1989 are for feed-forward neural networks. If we add an additional linear mapping to Eq (5), it would be $\frac{dh\_t}{dt} = W\_2\sigma(W\_1 h\_t + Ux\_t)$, which is not a commonly used RNN cell. This is also not clear whether our counterexamples can be approximated by this variant. 

> Second, the activation function applied in Eq (5) restricts the value range of the derivative compared to linear RNN. Thus, I would find it not really surprising that this, at some point, limits the approximation capacity of the ODE.

The activation function range is not the main issue for the approximation capacity. 

The range of the activation function is not the main restriction as we can rewrite the scaled RNN $\frac{dh\_t}{dt} = D \sigma(Wh\_t + Ux\_t)$ into $\frac{d (D^{-1}h\_t)}{dt} = \sigma(WD (D^{-1}h\_t) + Ux\_t)$. In the approximation sense, the scaling of activation functions does not change the set of hidden dynamics, therefore the approximation capacity remains the same. 

> Question regarding Proposition 4.1: Given that a tanh is just a "rescale" sigmoid, I wonder how the sigmoid activation is affected by the Proposition. Especially in Figure 2, the hard sigmoid seems to be working quite well.

If we relax the theoretical constraints and consider the hidden dynamics generated by tanh and sigmoid, it can be seen that: Any hidden dynamics that can be generated via tanh RNN can also be generated via a biased sigmoid RNN. 

Consider the dynamics of tanh RNN:
$$\frac{dh\_t^{\textrm{tanh}}}{dt} = \textrm{tanh}(Wh\_t^{\textrm{tanh}} + Ux\_t)$$
As we replace the tanh with sigmoid, we have:
$$\frac{dh\_t^{\textrm{tanh}}}{dt} = 2 \textrm{sigmoid}(2 Wh\_t^{\textrm{tanh}} + 2 Ux\_t) - \mathbf{1}$$
Here $\mathbf{1}$ means all-one column vector.

Then we can have:
$$\frac{d(h\_t^{\textrm{tanh}} + \mathbf{1})/2}{dt} = \textrm{sigmoid}(2 Wh\_t^{\textrm{tanh}} + 2 Ux\_t)$$
$$\frac{d(h\_t^{\textrm{tanh}} + \mathbf{1})/2}{dt} = \textrm{sigmoid}(4 W (h\_t^{\textrm{tanh}} + \mathbf{1})/2 + 2 Ux\_t - 2 W \mathbf{1})$$
These are the hidden dynamics that can be generated via a biased sigmoid RNN. Therefore the approximation capacity of sigmoid RNN should be similar to the tanh RNN. Thus the universal approximation result should also hold for sigmoid RNN. 

> I think this work extends Li et al. 2022 in a meaningful direction. The question for me is how significant this extension is. 

Thank you for your affirmative comment on our direction. This is the first study that we are aware of rigorously demonstrating that nonlinearity, compared with linear RNN, is not enough to change the memory pattern fundamentally, therefore, does not help mitigate long-memory problems. This long-memory problem is inherent to recurrent neural network structures.

content.summary_of_the_paper:
The paper studies Recurrent Neural Nets (RNNs) with nonlinear activations like tanh, hardtanh, sigmoid, ReLU and examines their representation/approximation capabilities in comparison to linear RNNs where the activations are linear functions.

The paper generalizes several results from previous works about the approximation capabilities of linear RNNs and primarily show that having the nonlinear activations is not that much more beneficial, in the sense that the so-called "curse of memory" still remains. 

"Curse of memory" refers to the previously-observed fact that linear RNNs in order to be able to approximate an input-output relationship, the latter must not have long-term dependencies, i.e., they must be characterized by a fast decaying memory property.

The main question of the paper is "can we establish similar results for the types of relations that are efficiently approximable by nonlinear RNNs"?

Briefly, the two main results established here are that firstly, nonlinear RNNs are able to encompass all functions that are efficiently representable with linear RNNs, and secondly, that nonlinearities do not help significantly more, in the sense that there are nonlinear functionals that cannot be approximated by the nonlinear RNNs, and that there are even linear functionals that on one hand can be approximated but on the other hand they also exhibit the exponentially decaying memory property.
content.strength_and_weaknesses:
The paper strengths are:
+ nice conceptual setting for understanding RNNs representation capabilities
+ covering many nonlinear activations functions, so the paper is not overly relying on properties of ReLU or some other activation
+ nice comparison to linear RNNs vs nonlinear RNNs and perhaps surprisingly the nonlinear RNNs do not constitute a significant improvement
+ they need to overcome several technical difficulties to extend from the linear RNN case
+ the second main result is satisfying since the also provid a linear target functional, cannot be represented unless it has fast decaying memory. 

The paper weaknesses are:
- the first of the two results, seems to be relatively not surprising. Perhaps, the authors can clarify why the first bullet in Section 4 is not obvious? The reviewer was confused since it seems that nonlinear RNNs can directly emulate a linear RNN by inputting the biases parameters of the nonlinear activations to be extremely positive, essentially then operating in the linear regime. What am I missing?
-the second result is a bit more surprising, but overall the curse of memory situation seems to be related more to the RNN intrinsic architecture rather than to the activations used. In other words, having the ability to represent long term relations from the input to the output, seems to be the main reason why RNNs suffer from representation capabilities and that this is not affected by the activations per se. (a priori this is what the reviewer believed, and of course the result kind of shows this, but it goes to say that perhaps it is not too surprising)
content.clarity,_quality,_novelty_and_reproducib:
Typos: page 5, bullet 2: "in Definition 3.1, cannot be" --> i think there is some grammar/syntax issue there perhaps you miss a "but" or a "yet".

-the fact that you deal with tanh, hardtanh etc, I would move it earlier on in the text of the intro, cause otherwise the reader is left wondering what is the "nonlinear activations" that you mention everywhere.
content.summary_of_the_review:
This is a nice contribution for the theory of RNNs. The overall message of the paper is that nonlinear RNNs are not that much stronger than linear RNNs, in terms of efficient approximation/representation of input-output sequences. Specifically, if a relationship is approximated by an RNN (whether linear or nonlinear) then it must exhibit fast decaying memory properties. 

The paper is interesting and has potential to yield further insights into the properties of RNNs. It provides evidence that RNNs, whether linear or nonlinear, they suffer from the curse of memory phenomenon. It would be nice to establish this in a more general framework somehow.

We thank the reviewers' nice comments. Since there is a problem with the proof (and the claim) in Section 4.2, although the main results in Sections 4.1 and 4.3 are still correct, this paper requires a major revision. We will withdraw this paper and further improve the result. 

> The first of the two results, seems to be relatively not surprising.

The first result (approximation of linear functionals by nonlinear RNNs) is an intuitive but non-trivial extension of the linear RNN case.  

Since the tanh function around 0 is smooth, the small linear region can be used to approximate the linear RNN's behavior. The scaling method we use is simple and intuitive. However, based on the structures of the nonlinear RNN, it is not trivial in the sense that the linear RNN hypothesis space is not directly contained in the nonlinear hypothesis space. Moreover, it is also non-trivial in the sense that the uniform-in-$t$ setting is a strong approximation setting. It still takes detailed treatment to show that nonlinear RNNs can approximate linear RNNs hypothesis space which is exactly subset of the targeted linear functionals. 
 
> The second result is a bit more surprising, but overall the curse of memory situation seems to be related more to the RNN intrinsic architecture rather than to the activations used. In other words, having the ability to represent long-term relations from the input to the output, seems to be the main reason why RNNs suffer from representation capabilities and that this is not affected by the activations per se. (a priori this is what the reviewer believed, and of course the result kind of shows this, but it goes to say that perhaps it is not too surprising)

We thank the reviewer for pointing out this nice observation. Yes, we believe the recurrent structures instead of the specific activation functions are the source of the curse of memory problems. In order to resolve the long-memory problem, our results indicate that probably selecting point-wise nonlinearity (activation function) is not enough. 

> Typos: page 5, bullet 2: "in Definition 3.1, cannot be" --> I think there is some grammar/syntax issue there perhaps you miss a "but" or a "yet".

Thank you for pointing out the grammar issue. We will modify the paper accordingly.

content.title: Reply to Reviewer GNHx
content.comment:
We thank the reviewers' nice comments. Since there is a problem with the proof (and the claim) in Section 4.2, although the main results in Sections 4.1 and 4.3 are still correct, this paper requires a major revision. We will withdraw this paper and further improve the result. 

> One of their two main contributions ("the hypothesis space of nonlinear RNNs is not smaller than the linear RNN hypothesis space") is quite obvious and trivial to prove. I would be surprised this wasn't known in the literature.

Our work is the first paper working on uniform approximation in the functional setting for nonlinear RNNs. This uniform-in-$t$ setting is different from the previous discrete time setting. There is no contradiction between results for different setting. Moreover, our result gives the rate estimation which is not known in previous literature.

As mentioned in the related work ([1], [2], [3]), there are several universal approximation theorems for RNN, but most of them considered the target functionals that derived from hidden dynamics $s\_{t+1} = g(s\_t, x\_t), y\_t = h(s\_{t+1})$. As we illustrated in the answer to the next question, such target functionals are a subset of the 

[1] Approximation of Dynamical System by Continuous Time Recurrent Neural Networks, Ken-ichi Funahashi, Yuichi Nakamura, 1993

[2] Universality of fully connected recurrent neural networks; Kenji Doya, 1993

[3] Modeling of Continuous Time Dynamical Systems with Input by Recurrent Neural Networks, Tommy W. S. Chow, Xiao-Dong Li, 2000

> The other contribution (about the limitations of nonlinear RNNs) seems to contradict previous work. For example [1]. Can the authors comment on this?

In (Anton and Hans, 2007) paper, they considered the approximation of nonlinear target functionals derived from hidden dynamics $s\_{t+1} = g(s\_t, x\_t), y\_t = h(s\_{t+1})$. These functionals are subsets of the nonlinear functionals we are considering in the paper. 

Clearly many functional relationship learning is just some general linear/nonlinear functionals. They need not and in practice, we cannot verify whether they can be generated by an underlying dynamical system or not. In fact, as is shown by (Li et al 2022), linear decaying-memory functionals that can be represented by linear dynamical systems ($s\_{t+1} = Ws\_t + Ux\_t, y\_{t+1}=c^\top s\_{t+1}$) must possess an exponentially decaying memory. In other words, linear functionals with non-exponentially decaying memory cannot be written into a linear dynamical system. 

Moreover, in the paper by [4], they established the universal approximation of nonlinear functionals by ReLU RNN in the $L_2$ metric, this setting is weaker than the uniform-in-$t$ setting in our paper. 

[4] Approximation Bounds for Random Neural Networks and Reservoir Systems; Lukas Gonon, Lyudmila Grigoryeva, Juan-Pablo Ortega, 2020

>  I spent quite some time trying to figure out this discrepancy, in particular with the proof of proposition 4.1 (Sec A.5). I think that proof is wrong. The only assumption on the relation of $\bar{H}$ and $\widetilde{H}$ is that their distance is bounded by the magnitude of $\widetilde{H}$. With this, I don't think the equation $\bar{H}\geq(1-\delta)\widetilde{H}$ holds.

We thank the reviewer for pointing out the unclear step. 
We check the proof and this inequality can be make exact. 
However, in the process we discover there is mistakes in the proof. 
After discussion with my co-authors, we believe this part require a major revision and we will withdraw. 

> The paper would greatly benefit by having some more intuitions, rather than just equations.

Thank you for the suggestion, we will add more intuitions in the future revision.

content.title: Reply to Reviewer 8vKV
content.comment:
We thank the reviewers' nice comments. Since there is a problem with the proof (and the claim) in Section 4.2, although the main results in Sections 4.1 and 4.3 are still correct, this paper requires a major revision. We will withdraw this paper and further improve the result. 

> Relation to practical applications is not clear.

This is a theory paper. Our result tells us point-wise nonlinearity is probably not enough to resolve the long-memory problem. This has already been observed in practice. Our paper is explaining rigorously the reasoning behind this phenomenon. 

> Results seem a bit incremental.

This is the first study that we are aware of rigorously demonstrating that nonlinearity does not help mitigate long-memory problems. 

The overlap with the previous work is the functional approximation setup, which is a mathematical formulation proven to be useful to compare various network architectures. The key formulation follows the previous work but the results do not. Instead, as far as we know, there is no approximation rate estimation in the nonlinear setting. This is the first nonlinear work and it's not incremental. 

> Only a few activations were considered. Results don't seem to be agnostic to the activation function.

We considered the most commonly used activation functions for RNN such as tanh and hardtanh.

content.title: Summary and decision to withdraw
content.comment:
Following the useful feedback from the Reviewers, we discover a problem in the demonstration of the counterexamples for nonlinear functionals by nonlinear RNNs. 
The counterexample is incorrect as we select an irregular nonlinear functional and the selection of $\epsilon$ should not depend on $\kappa$ and $t\_0$. 
Although the inequality mentioned by the Reviewer GNHx can be established solidly, the propositions in Section 4.2 are incorrect.

In summary, even though the results in Sections 4.1 and 4.3 for linear functionals are still correct, this paper requires a major revision. 
Therefore we decide to withdraw from the ICLR.
